extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters, television writers, students of dramatic writing, and fans studying Aaron Sorkin's craft
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative features for writing scripts in the manner associated with Aaron Sorkin — emphasizing rapid-fire dialogue, extended monologues, conversational 'walk-and-talk' scenes, repartee, and strong authorial voice while noting common criticisms. Useful for writers emulating or studying Sorkin's techniques for television and film.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial voice / Not written by committee
rubrics_metrics.description: "who have great ideas, but the scripts aren't written by committee."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a distinctive, singular writer's voice rather than diluting the script through committee-writing. Collaborate (e.g., with an executive producer or director), but preserve the primary authorial perspective and coherent tonal choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fast-paced dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Sorkin is recognized for his trademark fast-paced dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write quick, energetic exchanges that drive pace and character rhythm. Use tempo and cadence to build urgency and wit; ensure clarity so rapid lines don't obscure meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extended monologues / speeches
rubrics_metrics.description: Sorkin is recognized for ... extended monologues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long speeches and monologues are a frequent device; although 'speeches are normally avoided' in visual media, they can succeed if the dialogue is compelling and serves character/emotion. Avoid speeches that feel expository or unearned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Walk-and-talk staging
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'walk and talk' sequences consist of single tracking shots of long duration involving multiple characters engaging in conversation as they move through the set; characters enter and exit the conversation as the shot continues without any cuts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use continuous, mobile staging (long takes, tracking shots) to create dynamic conversational scenes. Plan blocking so characters naturally enter/exit dialogue; coordinate writing with direction and production to realize these sequences physically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memorable, quotable lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Sorkin is also known for writing memorable lines, such as 'You can't handle the truth!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft punchy, high-impact lines that can stand alone and resonate beyond the scene. Aim for clarity, rhetorical force, and emotional pinpointing to increase quotability without sacrificing realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repartee, small talk, and banter
rubrics_metrics.description: For television, one hallmark of Sorkin's writer's voice is the repartee that his characters engage in as they small talk and banter about whimsical events ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rapid-fire repartee and light, character-revealing small talk to humanize ensembles and to balance heavier plot material. Employ whimsical or offhand references to reveal relationships and tone, but ensure the banter advances character or theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscure popular-culture references
rubrics_metrics.description: Interject obscure popular culture references into conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scatter specific cultural references to add texture and specificity to dialogue; make sure references suit character, era, and audience comprehension. Avoid overreliance that dates the script or confuses viewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literate scripting (highly written prose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although his scripts are lauded for being literate, ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for elevated, well-crafted language and syntactic wit that reads like literary writing while remaining performable. Balance literary flourish with cinematic clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid being overwrought
rubrics_metrics.description: Sorkin has been criticized for often turning in scripts that are overwrought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of excess—too much rhetorical flourish, melodrama, or expository density. Trim scenes and lines that feel melodramatic or self-indulgent; prioritize emotional truth and structural economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of speeches is a risk that can pay off
rubrics_metrics.description: His mentor William Goldman has commented that normally in visual media speeches are avoided, but that Sorkin has a talent for dialogue and gets away with breaking this rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If employing long speeches or rhetorical stretches, ensure they are earned by character and delivered with exceptional dramatic tension and linguistic virtuosity. Without those qualities, speeches may feel inappropriate for visual storytelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of women — avoid one-dimensional roles
rubrics_metrics.description: His portrayal of women has been criticized ... female characters in his works often subordinate, written to support the main male characters, ditzy and incompetent or ostensibly professional while still being depicted as overly emotional and needing to be rescued by men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create fully realized, autonomous female characters with agency, complexity, and clear arcs. Avoid stereotypes that make female roles merely supportive, emotional, or in need of rescue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid repetitive reuse of lines
rubrics_metrics.description: A fan created a YouTube video compilation showing how Sorkin tended to reuse certain lines of dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for originality in phrasing and thematic expression across projects. Reusing distinctive lines or verbal tics too often can undercut perceived originality and invite critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writer–producer/director division of labor in TV
rubrics_metrics.description: Sorkin focuses on writing the scripts while Schlamme executive produces and occasionally directs; Schlamme will create the look of the shows, work with the other directors, discuss the scripts with Sorkin as soon as they are turned in, make design and casting decisions, and attend the budget meetings; Sorkin tends to stick strictly to writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On television, coordinate early with producers/directors: writers can concentrate on script and voice while producers/directors handle visual design, casting, and technical execution. Frequent script-to-production discussion helps align textual intentions with staging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the audience feel it's worth sitting through
rubrics_metrics.description: For me, the writing experience is very much like a date. ... I want it to have been worth it for everyone to sit through it for however long I ask them to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure pacing, emotional variety, and payoff across the runtime. Mix humor, intelligence, and darker elements appropriately so that viewers feel engaged and rewarded for their investment of time.
